newsitem.title: FRANCE: France Telecom to put Internet on the cable.
newsitem.headline: France Telecom to put Internet on the cable.

text.p: France Telecom said on Monday it would put the Internet on cable and digital satellite television and would make E-mail a feature of the French Minitel basic online service.

Gerard Eymery, head of the multimedia activities of the telecom operator, said he expected that in the year 2001 there would be two to three million subscribers to modern online services in France, compared to some 200,000 now.
France Telecom is in negotiations with Lyonnaise des Eaux unit Lyonnaise Communications about offering Internet services on digital television cable networks, he said.
The two companies are talking about establishing a 50/50 joint venture which would involve two-thirds of all cable networks in France, or one million subscribers.
The third cable operator, Generale de Videocommunication, is being put up for sale by Cie Generale des Eaux (CGE) as part of a deal with media group Havas and pay-television group Canal Plus.
"There have been some big movements in the industry recently, believe me there will be more to come," Eymery told journalists.

He said France Telecom was considering its options on what to do with its small stakes in Havas as well as Canal Plus and other companies related to Generale des Eaux, now that CGE was preparing for head-on competition in telecommunications and Internet access upon market liberalisation in 1998.
France Telecom will launch Internet services on its own cable networks in Saint Quentin en Yvelines, Metz and Marseille in 1997 and will expand it to the rest of its network in 1998.
It will not produce or develop any decoders or set-top boxes but test any machines on the market for compatibility, leaving it up to the consumer to select the preferred unit.
Meanwhile, it is setting up a joint venture with digital satellite television broadcaster Television Par Satellite (TPS) in order to make Internet access a feature of the TPS service offering.
Television cable networks could allow much higher capacity and speed for Internet access than the current phone lines permit.
France Telecom is also testing ASDL (asynchronous digital subscriber line) techniques to speed up Internet connections.
In content, France Telecom has the Wanadoo online service and has set up France Telecom Multimedia Edition to work on projects which will combine CD-ROMs with online features.

In a bid to bring the average French user in contact with Internet communications, France Telecom has launched an electronic mail service on Minitel, which will allow the 17 million users of Minitel to send and receive messages from people connected to the Internet.

The messages can be read on the Minitel with a personal access code, but at a later stage these messages are also available over the telephone -- a software programme can read electronic messages over the phone.
The programme has been tested to be fluent in French and can cope with messages in foreign languages. It will not translate them.
